text: The total number of surahs in the Holy Quran is
explanation: The Quran is divided into 114 surahs, beginning with Al-Fatiha and ending with An-Nas.

text: For ease of recitation the Holy Quran is divided into how many juz (paras)?
explanation: The Quran is divided into 30 juz of roughly equal length, a division commonly used for reciting the whole Quran during Ramadan.

text: The longest surah of the Holy Quran is
explanation: Surah Al-Baqarah, with 286 verses, is the longest surah and occupies most of the first two and a half juz.

text: The shortest surah of the Holy Quran is
explanation: Surah Al-Kawthar consists of only three short verses, making it the shortest surah of the Quran.

text: The first revelation received by the Holy Prophet (PBUH) consisted of the opening verses of
explanation: The first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq, beginning with 'Iqra bismi Rabbika', were the first revelation brought by Jibrael.

text: The first revelation was received by the Holy Prophet (PBUH) in
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) was engaged in seclusion in the Cave of Hira when Jibrael brought the first revelation.

text: The Cave of Hira is situated on the mountain known as
explanation: Hira is a cave on Jabal-un-Nur (the Mountain of Light) near Makkah, so named because revelation first descended there.

text: According to the commonly accepted classification, the number of Makki surahs in the Quran is
explanation: Of the 114 surahs, 86 were revealed before the migration and are classified as Makki.

text: According to the commonly accepted classification, the number of Madani surahs in the Quran is
explanation: Twenty-eight surahs were revealed after the migration to Madina and are therefore classified as Madani.

text: Makki surahs characteristically address the listeners with the phrase
explanation: Makki revelation generally addresses humanity at large with 'Ya ayyuhan-nas', while Madani revelation usually addresses the believers.

text: The only surah of the Quran that does not begin with Bismillah is
explanation: Surah At-Tawbah (Surah 9) is the sole surah that opens without the Bismillah.

text: In which surah does Bismillah occur twice?
explanation: Surah An-Naml has Bismillah at its opening and again within verse 30, quoted in the letter of Hazrat Sulaiman (AS) to the Queen of Sheba.

text: Which surah is described in Hadith as the heart of the Quran?
explanation: Surah Yasin is widely known as Qalb-ul-Quran, the heart of the Quran.

text: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) declared which surah equal in reward to one-third of the Quran?
explanation: Surah Al-Ikhlas sums up the doctrine of divine oneness and is described in Hadith as equal to a third of the Quran.

text: Which surah is popularly called Aroos-ul-Quran (the bride of the Quran)?
explanation: Surah Ar-Rahman is called Aroos-ul-Quran because of its beauty and its refrain enumerating the favours of Allah.

text: In Surah Ar-Rahman the verse 'Fa bi-ayyi ala-i Rabbikuma tukazziban' is repeated
explanation: The refrain questioning which favours of the Lord are denied occurs thirty-one times in Surah Ar-Rahman.

text: Ayat-ul-Kursi, described as the greatest verse of the Quran, is part of
explanation: Ayat-ul-Kursi is verse 255 of Surah Al-Baqarah.

text: The number of verses in Surah Al-Fatiha is
explanation: Surah Al-Fatiha has seven verses, which is why it is also called Sab'a Mathani, the seven oft-repeated verses.

text: Which surah is known as Umm-ul-Kitab (the mother of the Book)?
explanation: Surah Al-Fatiha is called Umm-ul-Kitab because it contains in summary the essential themes of the whole Quran.

text: The number of verses in Surah Al-Baqarah is
explanation: Surah Al-Baqarah contains 286 verses, more than any other surah.

text: The longest verse of the Holy Quran, known as Ayat-ud-Dayn, deals with
explanation: Verse 282 of Surah Al-Baqarah, the longest verse in the Quran, lays down rules for writing down loans and debts.

text: The Holy Quran was compiled into a single written volume during the caliphate of
explanation: The scattered written records of the Quran were gathered into one bound copy on the order of Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA).

text: Who first proposed to Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) that the Quran be collected in one volume?
explanation: Hazrat Umar (RA) pressed the Caliph to collect the Quran after many memorisers were killed in battle.

text: The compilation of the Quran in Hazrat Abu Bakr's time was prompted by heavy casualties among the huffaz in the Battle of
explanation: A large number of Quran memorisers were martyred fighting Musailima the liar at Yamama, which raised fears that the text could be lost.

text: The companion entrusted with the task of collecting the Quran into one volume was
explanation: Hazrat Zaid bin Thabit (RA), a scribe of revelation, headed the work of collection under both Abu Bakr (RA) and Uthman (RA).

text: The caliph who had standard copies of the Quran prepared and sent to the main centres of the Islamic state is titled Jami-ul-Quran; he was
explanation: Hazrat Uthman (RA) standardised the text on one dialect and distributed official copies, earning the title Jami-ul-Quran.

text: The first compiled volume of the Quran was kept in the custody of
explanation: After Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) and Hazrat Umar (RA), the compiled copy was preserved with Hazrat Hafsa (RA), and Hazrat Uthman (RA) later borrowed it as the basis of the standard text.

text: The revelation of the Holy Quran was completed over a period of about
explanation: Revelation continued for roughly 23 years, thirteen in Makkah and ten in Madina.

text: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) received the first revelation at the age of
explanation: Prophethood began when the Prophet (PBUH) was forty years old.

text: The angel appointed to bring revelation to the prophets is
explanation: Hazrat Jibrael (AS), also called Ruh-ul-Amin, is the angel of revelation.

text: According to the Quran, the month in which its revelation began is
explanation: Surah Al-Baqarah states that the Quran was sent down in the month of Ramadan.

text: Laylat-ul-Qadr is described as better than a thousand months in
explanation: Surah Al-Qadr states that the Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.

text: The Quranic verse 'This day I have perfected your religion for you' was revealed on the occasion of
explanation: This verse of Surah Al-Maidah was revealed at Arafat during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat-ul-Wida).

text: The word 'Quran' literally means
explanation: Quran is derived from the root qara'a, so it means recitation or that which is recited.

text: Al-Furqan, used as another name of the Holy Quran, means
options: The criterion between right and wrong
explanation: Al-Furqan denotes that which distinguishes truth from falsehood.

text: The written copy of the Holy Quran in book form is called
explanation: Mushaf is the term for the Quran as a bound written volume, hence Mushaf-e-Uthmani for the standard text.

text: For the purpose of reciting the whole Quran in a week it is divided into seven parts, each called a
explanation: The seven divisions used for weekly recitation are known as manzils.

text: The number of rukus in the Holy Quran is generally given as
explanation: The standard Mushaf marks 540 rukus, short sections used to divide surahs for recitation in Taraweeh.

text: The number of verses of prostration (sajda tilawat) in the Holy Quran is
explanation: Fourteen verses of the Quran are marked as verses of prostration, and prostration is made on reciting or hearing them.

text: The thirtieth and last juz of the Quran is popularly known as
explanation: The last juz is called Juz Amma after the opening words of Surah An-Naba, 'Amma yatasa'alun'.

text: The two surahs collectively known as Al-Muawwidhatain are
explanation: Surah Al-Falaq and Surah An-Nas are called Al-Muawwidhatain because both begin with seeking refuge with Allah.

text: The surah revealed in condemnation of the Prophet's uncle Abu Lahab is
explanation: Surah Al-Masad, also called Surah Al-Lahab, denounces Abu Lahab and his wife for their hostility to Islam.

text: Surah Al-Fil refers to the destruction of the army of
explanation: Surah Al-Fil describes how Allah destroyed Abraha's elephant army that came to demolish the Kabah.

text: The story of Hazrat Yusuf (AS) is narrated in the Quran as
explanation: Surah Yusuf calls its own narrative Ahsan-ul-Qasas, the most beautiful of stories.

text: The only surah of the Quran named after a woman is
explanation: Surah Maryam is named after Hazrat Maryam (AS), the mother of Hazrat Isa (AS).

text: Detailed rules for the distribution of inheritance are laid down mainly in
explanation: Surah An-Nisa specifies the fixed shares of heirs along with wider rules concerning women and the family.

text: The commandments regarding hijab and the punishment for slander were revealed in
explanation: Surah An-Nur contains the law of qazf (false accusation of unchastity) and the injunctions of modesty and veiling.

text: Surah Al-Anfal deals principally with the events and spoils of the Battle of
explanation: Surah Al-Anfal was revealed after Badr and settles the question of the distribution of war booty.

text: Surah Al-Ahzab takes its name from the confederate armies that besieged Madina in the Battle of
explanation: Al-Ahzab means the confederates, the allied tribes who laid siege to Madina in the Battle of the Trench.

text: Surah Al-Fath was revealed in connection with
explanation: The surah declares the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah to be a manifest victory for the Muslims.

text: Surah An-Nasr was revealed with reference to
explanation: Surah An-Nasr speaks of the help of Allah and the victory, and of people entering Islam in crowds after the conquest of Makkah.

text: The story of Ashab-e-Kahf (the People of the Cave) is narrated in
explanation: Surah Al-Kahf opens with the account of the youths who took refuge in a cave and slept for centuries.

text: Which surah does Hadith recommend for recitation on Friday?
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) encouraged reciting Surah Al-Kahf on Friday, promising light between the two Fridays.

text: The counsel of a wise man to his son on gratitude, prayer and humility forms the theme of
explanation: Surah Luqman records the advice of Luqman the Wise to his son, beginning with the prohibition of shirk.

text: The surah that lays down rules of social conduct such as avoiding suspicion, backbiting and mockery is
explanation: Surah Al-Hujurat is often called the surah of manners for its detailed code of Muslim social behaviour.

text: The central theme of Surah Al-Kafirun is
options: Complete disassociation from disbelief and its worship
The signs of the Day of Judgement
explanation: The surah rejects any compromise in worship between the Prophet (PBUH) and the polytheists of Makkah.

text: Surah Al-Ankabut takes its name from which creature?
explanation: Al-Ankabut means the spider, referring to the parable of the spider's frail house given in the surah.

text: The surah in which the word 'Allah' occurs in every verse is
explanation: Surah Al-Mujadila is distinguished by the fact that the name of Allah appears in each of its verses.

text: The first surah in the order of the Mushaf is
explanation: Surah Al-Fatiha stands first in the arrangement of the Quran, which is why it is called the opening.

text: The last surah in the order of the Mushaf is
explanation: Surah An-Nas is the 114th and final surah of the Quran.

text: A person who has committed the entire Quran to memory is called
explanation: Hafiz means guardian, and it is used for one who preserves the whole Quran in memory.

text: The science that lays down the rules for correct pronunciation in reciting the Quran is
explanation: Ilm-ut-Tajwid governs the articulation of letters and the lengths of vowels in Quranic recitation.

text: The branch of Quranic science that studies the occasions and circumstances of revelation is called
explanation: Asbab-un-Nuzul records the events in response to which particular verses were revealed, aiding correct interpretation.

text: In Quranic sciences, Nasikh and Mansukh refer to
options: The abrogating and the abrogated verses
The clear and the allegorical verses
The Makki and the Madani verses
The recited and the unrecited revelation
explanation: Nasikh is a verse whose ruling supersedes an earlier one, and Mansukh is the verse whose ruling is superseded.

text: Verses of the Quran whose meaning is clear and unambiguous are termed
explanation: Surah Aal-e-Imran divides the Quran into Muhkamat, the decisive verses, and Mutashabihat, those of allegorical meaning.

text: The explanation and exegesis of the Holy Quran is known as
explanation: Ilm-ut-Tafsir is the discipline devoted to explaining the meanings and implications of the Quranic text.

text: The mode of Quranic recitation followed by the great majority of Muslims today is transmitted as
explanation: The reading of Hafs on the authority of Asim is the standard recitation used in most printed Qurans, including those in Pakistan.

text: Wahi Matluww refers to
options: Revelation recited as the Quran in prayer
The rulings of the four imams
explanation: Wahi Matluww is the recited revelation, that is the Quran itself, as distinct from Wahi Ghair Matluww which reached the Prophet (PBUH) as Sunnah.

text: The number of books included in the Sihah Sitta is
explanation: Sihah Sitta means the six authentic collections of Hadith recognised by Sunni scholars.

text: The book regarded as the most authentic after the Holy Quran is
explanation: Sahih Bukhari occupies the first place among Hadith collections in authenticity in Sunni scholarship.

text: The compiler of Sahih Bukhari was
explanation: Imam Muhammad bin Ismail al-Bukhari compiled Al-Jami' as-Sahih, popularly known as Sahih Bukhari.

text: Imam Bukhari was born in the city of
explanation: He was born at Bukhara in Transoxiana, from which his nisbah al-Bukhari is derived.

text: Imam Bukhari died in the year
explanation: Imam Bukhari was born in 194 AH and died in 256 AH near Samarkand.

text: The compiler of Sahih Muslim was
explanation: Imam Muslim bin al-Hajjaj al-Qushayri of Nishapur compiled the collection known as Sahih Muslim.

text: Sunan Abu Dawud was compiled by
explanation: Abu Dawud Sulaiman bin Ash'ath as-Sijistani compiled the Sunan that bears his name, focused largely on legal Hadith.

text: The compiler of Jami' at-Tirmidhi was
explanation: Imam Abu Isa Muhammad bin Isa at-Tirmidhi compiled the Jami', noted for grading each Hadith.

text: The compiler of the sixth book of the Sihah Sitta, Sunan Ibn Majah, was
explanation: Imam Muhammad bin Yazid, known as Ibn Majah al-Qazwini, compiled the Sunan counted as the sixth canonical collection.

text: Al-Muwatta, one of the earliest surviving collections of Hadith and law, was compiled by
explanation: Imam Malik bin Anas of Madina compiled Al-Muwatta, which combines Hadith with the practice of the people of Madina.

text: The vast Hadith collection known as Al-Musnad was compiled by
explanation: Musnad Ahmad arranges tens of thousands of narrations under the names of the companions who related them.

text: Sahih Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are together referred to as
explanation: The two most authentic collections are jointly called the Sahihain.

text: A Hadith reported by both Imam Bukhari and Imam Muslim is described as
explanation: Muttafaq Alayh means agreed upon, that is recorded by both compilers of the Sahihain.

text: A Hadith reported in every generation by so many narrators that their agreement upon a falsehood is inconceivable is called
explanation: Mutawatir narrations enjoy the highest certainty because of the sheer number of independent transmitters at every stage.

text: Khabar-e-Wahid (Hadith Ahad) is a report that
options: Is narrated only by the Prophet's family
Falls short of the number required for tawatur
Is recorded only in Sahih Bukhari
explanation: Ahad reports are transmitted by fewer narrators than the mutawatir threshold, so they yield strong probability rather than certainty.

text: In Hadith terminology, Daif means a report that is
explanation: A Daif Hadith fails to meet the conditions of Sahih or Hasan, usually because of a defect in its chain or a criticised narrator.

text: A report falsely invented and attributed to the Holy Prophet (PBUH) is called
explanation: Maudu means fabricated, and such reports have no standing as Hadith at all.

text: A Hadith that meets every condition of authenticity, with an unbroken chain of upright and precise narrators and no defect, is classified as
explanation: Sahih is the highest grade of an accepted Hadith, and Hasan falls just below it because of slightly lesser precision in a narrator.

text: In Hadith terminology, the chain of narrators is called
explanation: Isnad, or sanad, is the succession of transmitters by which a report reaches the collector.

text: A Hadith Qudsi is one in which
options: The narration is traced only to a successor
Both the meaning and the wording are from a companion
The wording is recited in the obligatory prayers
The meaning is from Allah and the wording from the Prophet (PBUH)
explanation: In Hadith Qudsi the Prophet (PBUH) relates a statement from his Lord in his own words, unlike the Quran whose exact wording is revealed.

text: A narration whose chain reaches back to the Holy Prophet (PBUH) himself is termed
explanation: Marfu means raised, that is attributed to the Prophet (PBUH) in word, deed or approval.

text: A report whose chain stops at a companion and is attributed to him rather than to the Prophet (PBUH) is called
explanation: Mawquf means halted, because the narration goes no further than the saying or act of a sahabi.

text: A statement attributed to a tabi'i (successor) is classified as
explanation: Maqtu refers to the words or deeds of a successor, and should not be confused with Munqati, which describes a broken chain.

text: A Mursal Hadith is one in which
options: The narrator is accused of lying
A successor narrates directly from the Prophet (PBUH) without naming the companion
explanation: In a Mursal report the link of the sahabi is omitted, since a tabi'i attributes the Hadith straight to the Prophet (PBUH).

text: The science that examines the lives, reliability and dates of Hadith narrators is called
explanation: Ilm-ur-Rijal, the science of men, was developed to verify each transmitter in a chain of narration.

text: Al-Jarh wa at-Ta'dil is the discipline concerned with
options: Deriving legal rulings from the Quran
Determining the direction of the Qibla
Fixing the dates of the Islamic calendar
explanation: Jarh means to impugn a narrator and Ta'dil to declare him trustworthy, and together they decide whether a chain is acceptable.

text: A tacit approval given by the Holy Prophet (PBUH) to an act done in his presence is known as
explanation: Sunnah is divided into the Prophet's sayings, his deeds and his silent approvals, the last being Sunnat-e-Taqriri.

text: The companion who narrated the largest number of ahadith is
explanation: Hazrat Abu Hurairah (RA) is credited with more narrations than any other companion.

text: Among women, the largest number of ahadith has been narrated by
explanation: Hazrat Ayesha (RA) narrated more Hadith than any other woman and was a leading authority on the Prophet's private life and on fiqh.

text: The Hadith 'Actions are judged only by intentions' is narrated on the authority of
explanation: Hazrat Umar bin al-Khattab (RA) reported this Hadith from the pulpit, and it heads Sahih Bukhari.

text: The Hadith of Jibrael, in which the angel questions the Prophet (PBUH) in the presence of the companions, explains
explanation: In this Hadith Jibrael asks about Islam, Iman and Ihsan, and about the signs of the Hour, and the Prophet (PBUH) defines each.

text: According to a well-known Hadith recorded by Imam Muslim, 'At-tuhuru shatr-ul-iman' means
options: Modesty is a branch of faith
Prayer is the pillar of faith
explanation: The Hadith declares cleanliness or purification to be half of faith.

text: According to a Hadith of Sahih Bukhari, the best among the Muslims are those who
options: Learn the Quran and teach it
Spend the whole night in prayer
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said, 'The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.'

text: According to a well-known Hadith, a Muslim is one from whose
options: Wealth the poor are fed daily
Tongue and hand other Muslims are safe
Prayers no night is left empty
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) defined the Muslim as the person from whose tongue and hand other Muslims remain safe.

text: The Hadith 'Ad-Dinu an-Nasiha' means that religion is
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said religion is sincere advice, owed to Allah, His Book, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and the common people.

text: Sahifa Sadiqa, an early written record of Hadith, is attributed to
options: Hazrat Abdullah bin Amr bin al-As (RA)
explanation: Hazrat Abdullah bin Amr bin al-As (RA) wrote down ahadith with the Prophet's permission in a collection known as As-Sahifa as-Sadiqa.

text: A scholar specialising in the narration and criticism of Hadith is called
explanation: Muhaddith is the title for an expert in Hadith, as Mufassir is for an expert in Quranic exegesis.

text: In which year, traditionally known as the Year of the Elephant, was Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) born?
explanation: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was born in Mecca in 570 CE, the year an Abyssinian army with elephants attempted to attack the Kaaba.

text: What was the name of Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) father?
explanation: The Prophet's father, Abdullah ibn Abdul Muttalib, died before his birth.

text: What was the name of Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) mother?
explanation: Aminah bint Wahb was the Prophet's mother; she died when he was about six years old.

text: Who was the foster mother who nursed Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) in his infancy?
explanation: Halima Sa'diyya of the Banu Sa'd tribe nursed and raised the infant Prophet in the desert, following Meccan custom.

text: After the death of his mother, who took charge of raising the young Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
explanation: His grandfather Abdul Muttalib cared for him after Aminah's death, until his own death two years later.

text: After his grandfather's death, which uncle became the guardian of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
explanation: Abu Talib, the Prophet's paternal uncle, raised and protected him, including during the early years of his prophethood.

text: Before his prophethood, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was widely known among the Meccans by which title for his honesty?
explanation: He was called Al-Amin, meaning 'the Trustworthy', because of his reputation for honesty even before receiving revelation.

text: Who was the first wife of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
explanation: Khadija bint Khuwaylid, a wealthy Meccan merchant, married the Prophet and remained his only wife until her death.

text: At what age did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) receive his first revelation?
explanation: The Prophet was 40 years old when he received the first revelation in the Cave of Hira.

text: Who was the first woman to accept Islam?
explanation: Khadija, the Prophet's wife, was the first person of any gender to believe in his message.

text: Who was the first child to accept Islam?
explanation: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's young cousin living in his household, is traditionally regarded as the first child to accept Islam.

text: Who was the first freed slave to accept Islam?
explanation: Zaid bin Haritha, adopted into the Prophet's household, was the first among the freed slaves to embrace Islam.

text: Who was the first free adult man to accept Islam?
explanation: Abu Bakr, a close friend of the Prophet, is regarded as the first free adult male to accept Islam.

text: During the early Meccan period, on which hill did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) first publicly call the Quraysh to Islam?
explanation: The Prophet gathered the Quraysh at Mount Safa to deliver his first open, public call to Islam.

text: Persecuted Muslims in Mecca were advised by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) to migrate for refuge to which kingdom?
explanation: The Prophet sent a group of early Muslims to Abyssinia (Christian Ethiopia), known for its just ruler, to escape Meccan persecution.

text: Who was the ruler of Abyssinia who gave refuge to the early Muslim migrants?
explanation: The Negus, known in Arabic sources as An-Najashi, protected the Muslim migrants and refused to hand them over to the Quraysh.

text: Which year of Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) life is known as 'Aam-ul-Huzn' (the Year of Sorrow), marked by the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib?
explanation: The tenth year of prophethood brought the deaths of both Khadija and Abu Talib in close succession, hence the name 'Year of Sorrow'.

text: The night journey of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) from Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa is known as
explanation: Al-Isra refers to the miraculous night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem, which preceded the ascension (Miraj).

text: During the Miraj (ascension), how many daily prayers were made obligatory upon Muslims?
explanation: Although fifty prayers were initially prescribed, the number was eventually reduced to five obligatory daily prayers.

text: The first pledge of Aqabah was taken between Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and a group of people from which city?
explanation: Pilgrims from Yathrib met the Prophet at Aqabah near Mina and pledged to accept Islam, paving the way for the later Hijrah.

text: In which Gregorian year did the Hijrah (migration) of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) from Mecca to Medina take place?
explanation: The Hijrah took place in 622 CE and later became the starting point of the Islamic lunar calendar.

text: Who accompanied Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) during the migration (Hijrah) to Medina?
explanation: Abu Bakr accompanied the Prophet on the journey to Medina, sharing the risks of the migration with him.

text: In which cave did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and Abu Bakr take shelter during the Hijrah?
explanation: They hid for three days in the Cave of Thawr, south of Mecca, before continuing on to Medina.

text: Which was the first mosque built by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), on the outskirts of Medina during the Hijrah?
explanation: Masjid Quba was built just outside Medina and is regarded as the first mosque established in Islam.

text: In Medina, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) paired each migrant (Muhajir) with a local Ansari as brothers; this bond is known as
explanation: The Mawakhat (bond of brotherhood) linked Muhajireen and Ansar as brothers, helping the migrants settle in Medina.

text: In which year after Hijrah did the Battle of Badr take place?
explanation: The Battle of Badr, the first major battle between the Muslims and the Meccan Quraysh, was fought in 2 AH.

text: At the Battle of Badr, the Muslim army was heavily outnumbered by the Meccan Quraysh; the Muslims numbered approximately
explanation: The Muslim force at Badr numbered around 313 men against a much larger Quraysh army.

text: In which year after Hijrah did the Battle of Uhud take place?
explanation: The Battle of Uhud was fought in 3 AH, a year after the Muslim victory at Badr.

text: The Muslim setback at the Battle of Uhud is chiefly attributed to which action?
options: Archers leaving their assigned position on the hill
The Muslims being outnumbered ten to one
The Prophet's absence from the battlefield
A shortage of weapons among the Muslims
explanation: A group of archers left their post to gather spoils, exposing the Muslim rear and allowing the Quraysh cavalry to turn the battle.

text: Who suggested digging a trench around Medina to defend against the confederate forces in 5 AH?
explanation: Salman al-Farsi, familiar with Persian military tactics, proposed digging a trench to defend Medina.

text: The Battle of the Trench is also known as
explanation: The Battle of the Trench is also called Khandaq or Al-Ahzab, referring to the confederate tribes that besieged Medina.

text: In which year after Hijrah was the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah signed between the Muslims and the Quraysh?
explanation: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was signed in 6 AH, establishing a ten-year truce between the Muslims and the Quraysh.

text: In which year after Hijrah did the peaceful conquest of Mecca take place?
explanation: Mecca was conquered largely without bloodshed in 8 AH after the Quraysh violated the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.

text: At the conquest of Mecca, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) ordered the removal of how many idols from around the Kaaba, according to tradition?
explanation: Tradition holds that 360 idols surrounding the Kaaba were destroyed on the Prophet's orders after the conquest of Mecca.

text: Shortly after the conquest of Mecca, Muslim forces fought a confederation of Bedouin tribes at
explanation: The Battle of Hunayn, fought soon after the conquest of Mecca, was against the Hawazin and Thaqif tribal confederation.

text: The last military expedition personally led by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), directed toward the Byzantine frontier, was the
explanation: The Expedition of Tabuk, undertaken in response to rumours of a Byzantine advance, was the Prophet's final personally-led campaign.

text: In which year after Hijrah did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) perform his only and Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjatul Wida)?
explanation: The Prophet performed his only Hajj, known as the Farewell Pilgrimage, in 10 AH.

text: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) delivered his Farewell Sermon at
explanation: The Farewell Sermon was delivered on Mount Arafat during the Farewell Pilgrimage, setting out key principles of Islamic conduct.

text: In which year after Hijrah did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) pass away?
explanation: The Prophet passed away in Medina in 11 AH, shortly after completing the Farewell Pilgrimage.

text: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) is buried in Medina, in the chamber that had belonged to which of his wives?
explanation: The Prophet was buried in the room of his wife Aisha, adjoining Masjid-e-Nabvi in Medina.

text: Who was appointed by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) as the first muezzin to call the adhan?
explanation: Bilal ibn Rabah, a freed Abyssinian slave known for his beautiful voice, was chosen as the first muezzin in Islam.

text: Which uncle of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), titled 'Lion of Allah', was martyred at the Battle of Uhud?
explanation: Hamza ibn Abdul Muttalib, called Asadullah (Lion of Allah), was killed at Uhud and is remembered as a chief martyr of Islam.

text: In which year after Hijrah was the direction of prayer (Qibla) changed from Jerusalem to the Kaaba?
explanation: The Qibla was changed from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca in 2 AH, while the Prophet was praying in Medina.

text: Which companion, later known as 'Saifullah' (the Sword of Allah), commanded the Muslim army after the death of its three commanders at the Battle of Mu'tah?
explanation: Khalid bin Waleed took command at Mu'tah after the deaths of Zaid bin Haritha, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Abdullah ibn Rawaha, and skilfully led the army's withdrawal.

text: Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) mosque in Medina, built after the Hijrah, is known as
explanation: Masjid-e-Nabvi, built by the Prophet in Medina, became the central mosque of the early Muslim community.

text: The declaration 'La ilaha illallah Muhammadur Rasulullah' is known as
explanation: The Shahada is the testimony of faith affirming the oneness of God and the prophethood of Muhammad (PBUH), the first pillar of Islam.

text: According to Islamic law, Salah becomes obligatory on a Muslim upon reaching
explanation: Salah becomes obligatory once a Muslim of sound mind reaches puberty, though children are encouraged to practice it earlier.

text: How many obligatory (fard) prayers must a Muslim offer each day?
explanation: Muslims are obligated to perform five daily prayers: Fajr, Zuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha.

text: Which of the five daily prayers consists of only two obligatory rakats?
explanation: Fajr, the dawn prayer, consists of two obligatory rakats, fewer than the other daily prayers.

text: Muslims face which direction while performing Salah?
explanation: Muslims face the Kaaba in Mecca, the Qibla, during Salah, a direction fixed since the second year after Hijrah.

text: The ritual ablution performed before Salah is called
explanation: Wudu is the ritual washing of the face, arms, head, and feet performed before Salah.

text: When water is unavailable or unsafe to use, a Muslim may perform ritual purification using clean earth or sand; this is called
explanation: Tayammum is a dry ablution using clean earth, permitted when water is unavailable, insufficient, or harmful to use.

text: Zakat is obligatory on a Muslim's wealth once it equals or exceeds a minimum threshold known as
explanation: Nisab is the minimum amount of wealth a Muslim must own before Zakat becomes obligatory.

text: The standard rate of Zakat payable on qualifying savings and cash held for a full lunar year is
explanation: Zakat on savings and cash is generally calculated at 2.5% of the qualifying wealth.

text: Zakat becomes obligatory on savings after they remain in a Muslim's possession, above the nisab, for
explanation: Zakat is due once qualifying wealth above the nisab has been held for one complete lunar (Hijri) year.

text: Fasting (Sawm) is obligatory on Muslims during which month of the Islamic calendar?
explanation: Sawm, obligatory fasting from dawn to sunset, is observed throughout the month of Ramadan.

text: The pre-dawn meal eaten before beginning the daily fast in Ramadan is called
explanation: Suhoor is the meal taken before dawn, prior to starting the day's fast.

text: The meal with which a fasting Muslim breaks the fast at sunset is called
explanation: Iftar is the meal eaten at sunset to end the day's fast during Ramadan.

text: Performing Hajj is obligatory once in a lifetime on every adult Muslim who meets the condition of
explanation: Hajj is obligatory only on those who possess Istita'ah, meaning the physical health and financial means to undertake the journey.

text: The sacred state of consecration a pilgrim enters before performing Hajj or Umrah, marked by wearing simple unstitched garments, is called
explanation: Ihram is the state of ritual consecration a pilgrim enters, symbolised for men by wearing two plain unstitched sheets.

text: Hajj is performed during which Islamic month?
explanation: Hajj takes place during the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah, the final month of the Islamic calendar.

text: The ritual of circling the Kaaba seven times during Hajj or Umrah is called
explanation: Tawaf is the ritual circumambulation of the Kaaba, performed seven times in a counter-clockwise direction.

text: The ritual of walking briskly seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah during Hajj or Umrah is called
explanation: Sa'i commemorates Hajar's search for water and involves walking between Safa and Marwah seven times.

text: The symbolic stoning of pillars during Hajj, commemorating the rejection of Satan's temptation, is called
explanation: Ramy al-Jamarat involves throwing pebbles at three pillars in Mina, symbolising the rejection of Satan.

text: Unlike Hajj, which can only be performed at a fixed time of year, the minor pilgrimage that may be performed at any time is called
explanation: Umrah is a shorter, non-obligatory pilgrimage to Mecca that may be performed at any point during the year.

text: Which of the following correctly lists the Five Pillars of Islam?
explanation: The Five Pillars are Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj, the core obligatory acts of Islamic practice.

text: Which four schools of Fiqh (jurisprudence) are recognized within Sunni Islam?
explanation: The four major Sunni schools of jurisprudence are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali.

text: The Hanafi school of Fiqh was founded by
explanation: Imam Abu Hanifa founded the Hanafi school, which is the most widely followed school of Fiqh in South Asia.

text: The Maliki school of Fiqh takes its name from
explanation: The Maliki school is named after Imam Malik ibn Anas of Medina, author of the Muwatta.

text: The Shafi'i school of Fiqh was founded by
explanation: Imam Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i founded the Shafi'i school, known for systematising the principles of Islamic jurisprudence.

text: The Hanbali school of Fiqh takes its name from
explanation: The Hanbali school is named after Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, also known for his hadith compilation, the Musnad.

text: Which school of Fiqh is predominantly followed by Muslims in Pakistan?
explanation: The Hanafi school is the predominant school of Fiqh followed by the majority of Muslims in Pakistan.

text: In Islamic jurisprudence, an act that is obligatory and whose omission is sinful is termed
explanation: Fard denotes an act that is obligatory in Islamic law, such as the five daily prayers.

text: An act that the Prophet (PBUH) regularly practised but which is not strictly obligatory is termed
explanation: Sunnah refers to practices regularly followed by the Prophet (PBUH), recommended though not strictly obligatory.

text: According to the Hanafi school, the Witr prayer is generally regarded as
explanation: The Hanafi school considers Witr, offered after Isha, to be Wajib (necessary), distinguishing it from the other schools' views.

text: The congregational Friday prayer, obligatory on adult male Muslims, is called
explanation: Salat-ul-Jumu'ah is the obligatory congregational prayer performed by adult male Muslims on Fridays.

text: The Friday congregational prayer replaces which of the five daily obligatory prayers?
explanation: Jumu'ah prayer is performed in place of the Zuhr prayer on Fridays.

text: The charity that must be given by every Muslim before the Eid-ul-Fitr prayer is called
explanation: Sadaqah-tul-Fitr, also called Fitrana, must be given before the Eid-ul-Fitr prayer to ensure the needy can also celebrate.

text: The animal sacrifice performed by Muslims during Eid-ul-Adha, commemorating Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son, is called
explanation: Qurbani is the ritual animal sacrifice performed during Eid-ul-Adha in remembrance of Prophet Ibrahim's obedience.

text: The practice of retreating into a mosque for devotion, especially observed during the last ten days of Ramadan, is called
explanation: I'tikaf is a period of spiritual seclusion in the mosque, commonly observed during the last ten days of Ramadan.

text: Who became the first Caliph of Islam after the death of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
explanation: Abu Bakr was chosen as the first Caliph following the Prophet's death in 11 AH.

text: Abu Bakr is generally known by the title
explanation: Abu Bakr was given the title As-Siddiq (the Truthful) for his immediate belief in the Prophet's night journey and message.

text: The wars fought by Caliph Abu Bakr against tribes that renounced Islam or refused to pay Zakat after the Prophet's death are known as
explanation: The Ridda Wars were fought by Abu Bakr to suppress tribal rebellion and apostasy that broke out after the Prophet's death.

text: During the Ridda Wars, Muslim forces under Khalid bin Waleed defeated the false prophet Musaylimah at the
explanation: Khalid bin Waleed defeated Musaylimah's forces at the Battle of Yamama, ending one of the major Ridda rebellions.

text: The compilation of the Quran into a single written volume was first undertaken during the caliphate of
explanation: After many Quran reciters died in the Ridda Wars, Abu Bakr ordered the first compilation of the Quran into one volume.

text: Who was entrusted with compiling the written Quran into a single volume during Abu Bakr's caliphate?
explanation: Zaid ibn Thabit, a scribe of revelation, was tasked with collecting the Quran into a single written text.

text: Abu Bakr's caliphate lasted approximately
explanation: Abu Bakr ruled as Caliph for about two years, from 632 to 634 CE.

text: Before becoming Caliph, Abu Bakr was the father-in-law of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) through his daughter
explanation: Abu Bakr's daughter Aisha married the Prophet, making Abu Bakr his father-in-law.

text: Abu Bakr nominated which companion as his successor before his death?
explanation: Before his death, Abu Bakr nominated Umar ibn al-Khattab as the next Caliph.

text: Caliph Abu Bakr is buried in Medina beside
explanation: Abu Bakr is buried next to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) in the chamber that had belonged to Aisha.

text: The second Rightly-Guided Caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab, is commonly known by the title
explanation: Umar ibn al-Khattab was given the title Al-Farooq, meaning one who distinguishes truth from falsehood.

text: Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab was assassinated by
options: Abu Lu'lu'ah Firoz, a Persian slave
explanation: Umar was fatally stabbed by Abu Lu'lu'ah Firoz, a Persian slave, while leading the Fajr prayer.

text: The Islamic (Hijri) lunar calendar, taking the migration to Medina as its starting point, was formally adopted during the caliphate of
explanation: Umar ibn al-Khattab formally established the Hijri calendar, dating years from the Prophet's migration to Medina.

text: The decisive battle in which Muslim forces defeated the Sassanid Persian army, opening the way to Iraq, was the Battle of
explanation: The Battle of Qadisiyyah broke Sassanid resistance in Iraq and opened the way for the Muslim conquest of Persia.

text: The battle that broke the main Byzantine resistance in Syria, fought in 636 CE, was the Battle of
explanation: The Battle of Yarmouk, fought in 636 CE, decisively broke Byzantine power in Syria.

text: The battle sometimes called the 'Victory of Victories', which broke organized Sassanid resistance in Persia, was the Battle of
explanation: The Battle of Nahavand, fought under Umar's caliphate, is often called the 'Victory of Victories' for ending organized Persian resistance.

text: When Caliph Umar entered Jerusalem in 637 CE, he granted its Christian inhabitants a covenant guaranteeing their safety and property; this is known as
explanation: The Covenant of Umar guaranteed the safety, property, and freedom of worship of Jerusalem's Christian population.

text: Umar ibn al-Khattab was the first Caliph to adopt the title
explanation: Umar was the first to be addressed as Amir-ul-Momineen, meaning Commander of the Faithful.

text: Caliph Umar's administrative reforms included establishing a public treasury known as
explanation: Umar formally organized the Bait-ul-Mal, a public treasury used to administer state revenues and distribute stipends.

text: Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate lasted approximately
explanation: Umar ruled as Caliph for about ten years, from 634 to 644 CE, during which the Islamic state expanded rapidly.

text: Before his death, Caliph Umar appointed a council to choose his successor from among its members; this council is known as
explanation: Umar appointed a six-member Shura council to select the next Caliph from among themselves after his death.

text: The third Rightly-Guided Caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, is known by the title 'Dhun-Nurayn' (Possessor of Two Lights) because he married
options: Two of the Prophet's daughters, successively
explanation: Uthman married the Prophet's daughters Ruqayyah and, after her death, Umm Kulthum, earning him the title Dhun-Nurayn.

text: Caliph Uthman ibn Affan is chiefly remembered for
options: Compiling the first written copy of the Quran
Standardizing the text of the Quran into a single authoritative copy
explanation: Uthman is best remembered for standardizing the Quran's text and distributing authoritative copies to major cities.

text: The standardized copies of the Quran prepared under Caliph Uthman are known as
explanation: The standardized copies produced under Uthman are known as the Uthmanic codices, or Mushaf.

text: During his caliphate, Uthman ibn Affan carried out a significant expansion of
explanation: Uthman expanded and rebuilt Masjid-e-Nabvi in Medina to accommodate the growing Muslim community.

text: Uthman ibn Affan's caliphate lasted approximately
explanation: Uthman ruled as Caliph for about twelve years, from 644 to 656 CE.

text: Caliph Uthman ibn Affan was assassinated by
options: Rebels who besieged his house in Medina
explanation: Uthman was killed by rebels who besieged his house in Medina and forced their way in while he was reading the Quran.

text: Caliph Uthman ibn Affan is credited with establishing the first organized
explanation: Uthman authorized the building of the first organized Muslim naval fleet, used in campaigns such as the conquest of Cyprus.

text: The fourth Rightly-Guided Caliph, Ali ibn Abi Talib, was married to Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) daughter
explanation: Ali ibn Abi Talib was married to Fatima, the Prophet's youngest daughter.

text: Caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib moved the seat of the caliphate from Medina to
explanation: Ali relocated the capital of the caliphate to Kufa in present-day Iraq.

text: The battle fought between Caliph Ali and a force led by Aisha, Talha, and Zubayr is known as the
explanation: The Battle of the Camel, named for the camel Aisha rode during the fighting, was fought between Ali's forces and those of Aisha, Talha, and Zubayr.

text: The battle fought between the forces of Caliph Ali and Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan in 657 CE is known as the
explanation: The Battle of Siffin was fought between Ali's forces and those of Muawiyah, ending inconclusively with an arbitration agreement.

text: The group that broke away from Ali's camp after rejecting the arbitration following the Battle of Siffin became known as the
explanation: The Kharijites rejected the outcome of the arbitration after Siffin and turned against both Ali and Muawiyah.

text: Caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib was assassinated by
options: A Kharijite, Abdur Rahman ibn Muljam
explanation: Ali was fatally wounded by the Kharijite Abdur Rahman ibn Muljam while praying in the mosque at Kufa.

text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's caliphate lasted approximately
explanation: Ali ruled as Caliph for about five years, from 656 to 661 CE, a period marked by internal conflict.

text: The four Caliphs who ruled after Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), regarded as having followed his example most closely, are collectively called
explanation: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali are together known as the Khulafa-e-Rashideen, the Rightly-Guided Caliphs.

text: The correct chronological order of the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs is
explanation: The Rightly-Guided Caliphs ruled in the order Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and then Ali.

text: The era of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs came to an end and was succeeded by which dynasty, established by Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan?
explanation: After Ali's death, Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan established the Umayyad dynasty, ending the Rashidun era.

text: Taken together, the reigns of the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs spanned a total of approximately
explanation: From Abu Bakr's accession in 632 CE to Ali's death in 661 CE, the Rashidun era lasted about 29 years.

text: Under which Caliph was the conquest of the Sassanid Persian Empire substantially completed?
explanation: The decisive victories at Qadisiyyah and Nahavand under Umar's caliphate broke organized Sassanid resistance in Persia.

text: The branch of philosophy concerned with moral principles that govern a person's behaviour is called
explanation: Ethics is the study of moral principles that determine right and wrong conduct.

text: Regularly paying one's taxes and obeying the law of the land are examples of
explanation: Paying taxes and obeying the law are basic civic responsibilities expected of every citizen.

text: An awareness of one's duties toward the community and public property, such as keeping public spaces clean, is generally described as
explanation: Civic sense refers to an individual's awareness of and respect for shared community responsibilities and public property.

text: The principle that no one, including the government, is above the law, and that all are treated equally under it, is known as
explanation: The rule of law holds that all individuals and institutions, including the state, are subject to and equal before the law.

text: Unlike laws, which are enforced by the state, moral principles concerning right and wrong conduct are primarily enforced through
explanation: Moral principles are generally upheld through personal conscience and social approval or disapproval, rather than formal legal enforcement.

text: A system of government in which political power ultimately rests with the citizens, typically exercised through elected representatives, is called
explanation: Democracy is a system of government in which power ultimately rests with the citizens, usually exercised through elected representatives.

text: Basic entitlements guaranteed to every citizen, such as the right to life, equality, and freedom of expression, are known as
explanation: Fundamental rights are basic entitlements guaranteed to citizens, such as the right to life, equality, and free expression.

text: Which of the following is generally considered a duty of a responsible citizen, rather than a right?
options: Obeying the law and respecting the rights of others
explanation: Obeying the law and respecting the rights of others are civic duties expected of citizens, distinct from their guaranteed rights.

text: Accepting and respecting beliefs, practices, and ways of life that differ from one's own, especially in a diverse society, reflects the value of
explanation: Tolerance is the willingness to accept and respect beliefs and practices that differ from one's own.

text: Speaking and acting truthfully, and keeping one's promises, reflects the moral value of
explanation: Honesty and integrity involve consistently speaking the truth and honouring one's commitments.

text: The ethical principle of treating others as one would wish to be treated is commonly known as
explanation: The Golden Rule is the ethical principle of treating others the way one would wish to be treated.

text: Fair and impartial treatment of individuals, ensuring that everyone receives what they are due, defines the value of
explanation: Justice refers to fair and impartial treatment, ensuring individuals receive what is rightfully due to them.

text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in
explanation: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1948.

text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by which international body?
explanation: The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

text: Practices such as conserving water, reducing waste, and protecting public parks are examples of
explanation: Conserving resources and protecting shared public spaces are examples of environmental civic responsibility.

text: The misuse of public office or entrusted power for private gain is defined as
explanation: Corruption is the misuse of public office or entrusted authority for personal or private benefit.

text: Freely offering one's time and effort to help the community without expecting payment is known as
explanation: Volunteerism is the practice of freely giving one's time and effort to benefit the community without financial reward.

text: The central religious figure of Christianity, regarded by its followers as the Son of God and the Messiah, is
explanation: Jesus Christ is the central figure of Christianity, regarded by Christians as the Son of God and the Messiah.

text: The primary sacred scripture of Christianity is the
explanation: The Bible, comprising the Old and New Testaments, is the primary sacred scripture of Christianity.

text: The place of communal worship for Christians is called a
explanation: A church is the place of communal worship for followers of Christianity.

text: The primary sacred scripture of Judaism is the
explanation: The Torah, comprising the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, is the primary sacred scripture of Judaism.

text: The place of worship for followers of Judaism is called a
explanation: A synagogue is the place of communal worship and study for followers of Judaism.

text: The ancient sacred texts that form the oldest scriptures of Hinduism are known as the
explanation: The Vedas are the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism, forming the foundation of later Hindu texts.

text: The Hindu belief that the soul is repeatedly reborn into new bodies after death is called
explanation: Samsara is the Hindu belief in the cycle of rebirth, in which the soul is repeatedly reborn into new bodies.

text: The place of worship for followers of Hinduism is commonly called a
explanation: A temple, or mandir, is the common place of worship for followers of Hinduism.

text: Buddhism was founded by
explanation: Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama, who came to be known as the Buddha, or 'the Enlightened One'.

text: Siddhartha Gautama, the founder of Buddhism, is traditionally said to have been born in
explanation: Siddhartha Gautama is traditionally held to have been born in Lumbini, in present-day Nepal.

text: Sikhism was founded in the Punjab region by
explanation: Guru Nanak founded Sikhism in the Punjab region in the late fifteenth century.

text: The primary scripture of Sikhism, revered as the eternal living Guru, is the
explanation: The Guru Granth Sahib is the central scripture of Sikhism, revered by Sikhs as their eternal living Guru.

text: The ancient religion founded by the Persian prophet Zoroaster, whose sacred text is the Avesta, is known as
explanation: Zoroastrianism, founded by the Persian prophet Zoroaster, has the Avesta as its sacred scripture.
